A tall, flat, triangular pointer (the gnomon) stands in the middle and casts a blue shadow across the plate towards the numbers 10 to 12. The tip of the shadow lies near the lines for 10 and 11, and the pointer itself lies near 12 and 1.
figures.original: Look at the picture. Can you tell what time it is?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: A large yellow Sun with short black rays around it sits at the top of a blue background. A small Earth, with green land, blue sea and white at the pole, is drawn below the Sun. A large black circular arrow goes around the Earth and the Sun, starting near the Sun's lower left, passing under the Earth and ending with an arrowhead at the right of the Sun.
figures.original: Which picture is right, A or B?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: Three cartoon children stand side by side: one in a green top and blue trousers, one in an orange top and olive trousers with hands on hips, and one in a yellow top with a red star and dark trousers. Each child has a very long dark shadow that stretches down toward the bottom of the picture. The letter B is in the top left corner.
figures.original: Look at these pictures. a Is the Sun high or low in these pictures? b Do you think it is morning, midday or evening?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Two panels show an investigation with three small green seedlings in black pots next to a window with a bright sun. In the left panel, labelled "light", an open cardboard box stands beside the pots and the plants are in the light. In the right panel, labelled "no light", the box is turned over and moved down over the pots, shown by a red arrow, so the plants are covered and get no light.
figures.original: Look at the pictures to see what to do.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Three panels each show three small green seedlings in black pots and a green watering can, with a row of day letters m t w t f s s. In the first panel all seven days are ticked, and the caption is 'Water every day.' In the second panel only two days (Monday and Thursday) are ticked, and the caption is 'Water twice a week.' In the third panel the watering can is crossed out in red and no days are ticked, and the caption is 'Do not water.'
figures.original: Look at the pictures to see what to do. What do you predict will happen to the plants' leaves, stems and roots in each case?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a model flower made from craft materials. It has a yellow flower head with five pointed petals and an orange circular centre, on a white stem. Two green leaves are tied to the stem with thread, and loose grey threads hang from the bottom of the stem as roots. No labels are printed.
figures.original: Make a plant like this one.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a flowering plant with purple petals around a yellow centre, a green stem with four green leaves, and branching roots. Four labelled lines point to parts: D points to a petal of the flower, C points to a leaf on the right side, B points to the stem, and A points to a root.
figures.original: Here is a flowering plant. Copy and complete these sentences. A is the ______. B is the ______. C is a ______. D is the ______.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A four-panel chart with a blue border. Each panel has a word label and a picture: 'water' with a jug of water, 'light' with a yellow sun, 'food' with a loaf of bread and slices, and 'plant pot' with a dark plant pot.
figures.original: Which two of these does a plant need for it to to grow?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Three numbered cartoon panels show an experiment. In panel 1 a girl places half an egg shell into each of two cups. In panel 2 she pours water into one cup and a sugary drink from a bottle into the other. In panel 3, after seven days, she holds the cup with the sugary drink and looks at a crumbling egg shell, while the other cup stays on the table.
labels: Place half an egg shell into each cup.
Add water to one cup and a sugary drink to the other.
After seven days see what has happened to the egg shell.
figures.original: Look at the pictures to see what to do. Predict what you think will happen to the egg shells.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with the column headings 'Fruit/Vegetable', 'Prediction' and 'Result'. Under Prediction is 'Will you like it?'. Under Result are 'How did it taste?' and 'Did you like it?'. One row is filled in: melon, no, very sweet, yes. One blank row is below it.
figures.original: Draw a table like this for your results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A colored drawing of a meal on a green mat. A plate holds spaghetti topped with red tomato sauce and green basil leaves, with a fork on the left of the plate and a knife on the right. An orange sits at the upper left and a glass of water sits at the upper right. Nothing is labelled.
figures.original: Here is a healthy meal. Explain why it is healthy.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Two cartoon-style drawings of sandwiches labelled A and B. Sandwich A has yellow bread with lettuce leaves and tomato slices between the slices. Sandwich B has white bread with a dark red jam-like spread oozing out of the filling.
figures.original: Which sandwich is more healthy? Why?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Four drinks are drawn, each with a label giving its sugar content per 100ml. A water bottle says sugar 0g, a red cola can says sugar 11g, an orange carton with a blue straw says sugar 10g, and a purple blackcurrant carton says sugar 5g.
figures.original: These drinks have different amounts of sugar per 100ml.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Eight circular photographs with coloured borders, in two rows of four. The top row shows a burning match, a macaw flying, a stone moai statue on a grassy hill, and a tree covered in white blossom. The bottom row shows a space shuttle launching with a trail of flame, a pink jellyfish in water, a peacock butterfly on yellow flowers, and a desktop computer monitor with a keyboard and mouse.
figures.original: Which things in these pictures are alive?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A cartoon zookeeper in a green shirt with a 'Z' badge stands thinking, with thought bubbles around her showing eight animal heads: a lion, a swan, a mouse, a pelican, a lizard or snake-like reptile, a panda, an eagle and a crocodile. Below her are three cages with signs reading 'Animals with feathers', 'Animals with fur' and 'Animals with scales'.
figures.original: Help the zookeeper sort the animals into the correct group.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Two rows of six colored square cards, each with a drawing of a living thing. The top row shows a blue butterfly, a brown bear, a blue lupin plant with a flower spike, a black ant, a red flower with green leaves, and a yellow-gold fish. The bottom row shows a brown monkey, a small green-yellow fish, a brown scorpion, a silver spotted fish, a white goat, and a green plant with yellow flowers.
figures.original: Look at these pictures. Talk to a friend about how you could sort these living things.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A photograph of two large grey-blue herons at a nest made of sticks and twigs among green leaves. One heron stands upright behind with a long yellow beak, and the other leans forward over the nest with its neck stretched down, touching the sticks with its beak. The photo is set in a circular frame with a purple border.
figures.original: Name an animal and the shelter it makes for its eggs or young.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Three circular close-ups of fingerprints, each with a coloured border and a label beneath it. The left one, with a blue border, is labelled 'loop'. The middle one, with a pink border, is labelled 'arch'. The right one, with a green border, is labelled 'whorl'.
figures.original: Look at your fingers. Use a magnifying glass if possible. Identify which type of fingerprint you have.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A two-column table with the headings "Animal" and "Number of young produced". The rows are: rabbit, 8; birds, 6; human, 1 or 2; fish, 1000s of eggs; spiders, 100s of eggs.
figures.original: Which animals can have the most young?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a rose plant growing in a brown flowerpot. It has one green stem with several green leaves and a single red flower at the top. The pot is filled with brown soil. There are no labels.
figures.original: For this plant, which questions are 'true' and which questions are 'false'?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Eight colored square cards, each with one cartoon-style drawing. The top row shows a boy in a red and white striped shirt, a brown bear, a mouse, and a blue and purple butterfly. The bottom row shows a monkey, a white goat, a lion, and a grey elephant.
figures.original: Which of these animals do you think can smell things the best?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Eight separate colour drawings with no labels: a cuckoo clock, an eagle in flight, a lit tealight candle, a yellow Volkswagen Beetle car, a green frog with dark spots, and a yellow-flowered dandelion plant. Below these are a white cloud and a yellow sun partly covered by streaks of cloud.
figures.original: Magda's book contains pictures of these things. Help her to say which are alive and which are not alive.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed 'Material' and 'Properties'. The first row has 'paper' under Material and 'weak, flexible, smooth, absorbent' under Properties. The second row is empty.
figures.original: Draw a table like this and write down the properties of the materials.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A bar chart titled by its axes: the vertical axis is 'Number of children' with gridlines at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, and the horizontal axis is 'Eye colour'. There are three bars: grey is about 13, brown is about 41, and blue is about 38.
figures.original: Alex has recorded the eye colour of the children in his school on this graph. a Which is the most common eye colour? b Which is the least common eye colour?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with columns Name, Food, Like and Dislike, listing four children, each with apple and biscuit rows. Bill, Jaffa and Rava have a tick under Like for both apple and biscuit. Pat has a tick under Dislike for apple and a tick under Like for biscuit.
figures.original: a Which food is most popular?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A photograph of a life-size car sculpted entirely from clear, pale blue ice. It sits on a dark display platform at what looks like a car show, with a blue backdrop and a Ford logo at the right edge. The car is a convertible with an open top, and its wheels are also made of ice.
figures.original: Why is a car made of ice a silly idea?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A branching sorting chart (decision tree) starting with the question "Is it hard?" with yes and no arrows. The yes arrow leads to "Is it shiny?" and the no arrow leads to "Is it waterproof?". Each of these has yes and no arrows that end in empty question marks. A yellow side panel lists four objects with pictures: brick, balloon, paper (shown as a tissue box) and ice (a melting ice cube).
figures.original: Choose one of the four objects and answer the questions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A Venn diagram made of two overlapping circles. The left circle is labelled "flexible" and the right circle is labelled "hard". The overlap is empty, and so are the rest of both circles.
figures.original: Copy this Venn diagram and write the following objects in the right places.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A hand holds a red horseshoe magnet with grey tips, and the tips point to the right. Wavy lines next to each tip show the magnetic pull. A red toy car with blue-grey windows and wheels sits to the right of the magnet, facing right, with its back end toward the magnet.
figures.original: Draw a picture to show what will happen to the metal toy car.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed Object, Magnetic and Non-magnetic. The Object column has four rows, each with a label and a drawing: a metal can, a book, a football and metal scissors. The Magnetic and Non-magnetic cells are all empty.
figures.original: Copy and complete this table.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with four column headings: Object, Material, Magnetic and Non-magnetic. The one filled row reads chair, plastic, with a red tick in the Non-magnetic column and the Magnetic column left empty.
figures.original: Draw a table like this one for your results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A bar chart with the vertical axis 'Force in newtons (N)' numbered 0 to 5 and the horizontal axis 'Type of surface'. There are three bars. Wood is a brown bar at about 1.5 N, grass is a green bar at about 3.5 N, and stone is a grey bar at about 1 N.
figures.original: Which surface was the hardest to pull the skateboard on?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: Three forcemeters (newton meters) labelled A, B and C, each with a ring at the top, a red adjuster, a vertical slot with a scale of tick marks, and a hook at the bottom. Each has a yellow marker band with a value: A shows 5N, B shows 10N and C shows 20N. The yellow band sits higher on A, lower on B and lowest on C, near the bottom of the slot.
figures.original: Which forcemeter is measuring the greatest force?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A partly drawn bar chart with the vertical axis 'Plant height in cm' numbered 0 to 10. The first bar, 'Plant with water', has its top drawn at 8 cm, with its left and right sides drawn in black. A pencil points at the bottom of the right side at 2 cm. The second category, 'Plant with no water', has no bar drawn.
figures.original: Draw the sides of the first bar. Use a ruler.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A bar chart on lined paper with the vertical axis 'Plant height in cm' numbered 0 to 10. The bar for 'Plant with water' is drawn up to 8 cm. The bar for 'Plant with no water' is drawn up to 4 cm, with a pencil at its bottom right corner.
figures.original: Draw the second bar the same way. Use a ruler.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 3 Learners
figures.shows: A table with two columns and one row of data. The left column is headed "Plant height with water in cm" and holds the value 8. The right column is headed "Plant height with no water in cm" and holds the value 4.
labels: Plant height with water in cm
Plant height with no water in cm
figures.original: Look at the table. The numbers tell you how tall to make each bar.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed Josie, Yasmin and Luisa, and one row labelled 'Bone length in cm'. The values are 25 for Josie, 32 for Yasmin and 28 for Luisa.
figures.original: Josie, Yasmin and Luisa measured the length of their upper arm bones. These are their results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a bent human arm showing the bones of the shoulder, upper arm and forearm with two muscles on the upper arm. Label 1 points to the muscle on the front of the upper arm, and label 2 points to the muscle on the back of the upper arm. The forearm is bent at the elbow.
figures.original: Look at the drawing and answer the questions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: Six cartoon-style drawings of animals, each on a coloured square in two rows of three. Top row: a brown mouse on green, a brown rabbit on purple, a patterned grey and brown snake coiled on pale blue. Bottom row: a goldfish in a round fish bowl on red, a white and brown cat sitting on blue, a small brown rodent with a long tufted tail on red.
figures.original: Construct a key to identify these pets.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A bar chart with the vertical axis labelled 'Manure in tonnes', running from 0 to 20 in steps of 5. The horizontal axis lists the days Sunday to Saturday. Bar heights are: Sunday about 18, Monday 15, Tuesday 20, Wednesday 10, Thursday no bar (0), Friday 20, Saturday 15.
figures.original: Each day, Tabansi the farmer dumps manure from his animals on the land next to the river. The bar chart shows how many tonnes he dumps each day in one week.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: Four drawings, each inside a screen-like frame, arranged in a 2 by 2 grid. Top left: two fish swim in water among green water plants, with rocks on the bottom. Top right: a camel stands on yellow sand dunes under a bright sun, with a small spiky plant beside it. Bottom left: a green spotted frog sits on grass beside a pond with reeds and white flowers. Bottom right: a bald eagle with wings spread flies in front of a snow-capped mountain.
figures.original: Write the name of the habitat shown in each picture.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A particle model with 13 identical blue spheres on a white background. The spheres are spread far apart in an irregular, random arrangement, and none of them touch. There are no labels or printed values.
figures.original: Does the diagram below represent a model of a solid, a liquid or a gas?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: An old-fashioned gramophone (phonograph) in an oval frame. It has a square, dark patterned wooden box with a round turntable on top, a small label on the front and a hand crank on the right side. A curved arm holds a needle over the turntable and leads up to a large brass horn that flares outwards.
figures.original: Look at the picture. How do you think the music was made louder?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed 'Material' and 'Loudness of sound'. The Material column lists air, water and wood in three rows. The 'Loudness of sound' cells are all empty, to be filled in by the learner.
figures.original: Which material did you hear the sound best through?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: Three musical instruments are drawn and labelled A, B and C. A is a pair of yellow cymbals, each with a brown leather strap. B is a grey-blue woodwind instrument with a white mouthpiece, a row of finger holes and cream-coloured rings. C is a yellow harp with a tall pillar, a curved top and many vertical strings.
figures.original: Look at the pictures of these musical instruments.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of a tambourine, a round musical instrument with a wooden frame, a skin head and metal jingles set into the rim. A person's hand with a ring on one finger rests on the skin head. The caption below reads 'tambourine'.
figures.original: Look at each of these instruments. Which of these have you seen and heard?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: Eight identical glass bottles stand in a row on a line, numbered 1 to 8 below. Bottle 1 has a little water, and the water level rises in each bottle up to bottle 8, which is almost full. A bracket at the left marks the 'Column of air' above the water in bottle 1. Callouts say to pour a little water into bottle 1, a little more into bottle 2, and that bottle 8 must be almost full.
labels: Pour a little water into this bottle.
Pour a little more water into this bottle.
This bottle must be almost full.
figures.original: Predict what pitch of sounds you will make when you blow across the other bottles.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A battery lies on its side with its negative (−) end on the left and its positive (+) end on the right. A piece of tape holds one end of an orange wire to the + end. The wire runs in a loop to one terminal of a bulb holder, with arrows along the wire pointing from the + end towards the bulb. A second wire goes from the other terminal of the bulb holder back to the − end of the battery. The yellow bulb sits on a teal stepped base. The wire is attached to the − end only by its position, with no tape shown there. The arrows show the direction along the whole loop, from the battery's + end, through the bulb, and back to the − end.
figures.original: Look at the diagram. Predict what will happen to the bulb in this circuit.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A cutaway diagram of the inside of a torch. Two cells are stacked one above the other, each with a yellow + end at the top and a grey - end at the bottom. A bulb sits at the top inside a reflector, with labels pointing to the 'bulb' and the 'cell'. A yellow metal strip, a switch and a spring at the bottom complete the circuit. Arrows show the current going up the side strip, across the top to the bulb, and then down through the cells.
labels: The inside of a torch. The arrows show which way the electric current goes.
figures.original: What happens if you put the two positive terminals of the cells in a torch together? Will the bulb light up?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A series circuit drawn as apparatus: a battery pack of cells held together with tape, with a plus sign on one end, is joined by orange wires to a switch made from a wooden block with a paper clip and two drawing pins. The circuit continues through three bulbs, each on a green stepped holder, in a single loop back to the battery. The switch is drawn with the paper clip touching one pin at its end, and no bulbs are shown lit. The figure is marked with the number 1.
figures.original: Close the switch. Observe the bulbs. Open the switch.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a series circuit with a battery (cell) taped in a holder with the + end at the left, and two bulbs on green round bulb holders. Orange wires join the battery to the first bulb holder, the first bulb holder to the second bulb holder, and the second bulb holder to a wooden block switch. The switch is made from a paper clip and two metal fasteners (drawing pins). A wire from the switch returns to the battery's + end at the left.
figures.original: Describe the path of the electricity in the circuit you made.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A yellow ruler marked 0 to 15 is drawn along the bottom, with a bar magnet above it. The magnet's left half is red and labelled N, and its right half is blue and labelled S. A paperclip touches the N end of the magnet, with its left end near the 6 mark and the magnet spanning roughly 7 to 12 on the ruler. A black arrow at the top points toward the magnet.
figures.original: Stop the magnet as soon as the paperclip is attracted to and touches the magnet. Read off the distance in mm on the ruler. This is the first reading.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a series electric circuit. A battery with its minus end on the left and its plus end on the right is connected by orange wires to two lamps on teal bases, and to a switch on a wooden block. The switch is labelled A and has two metal contacts joined by a metal clip. All the parts are joined in one loop.
figures.original: In the circuit below:

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 4 Learners
figures.shows: A drawing of a simple electric circuit. A cell with its + end at the top left and its − end on the right is held with tape. Orange wires connect the cell to a switch made of a paper clip and two metal fasteners on a wooden block, and to a buzzer. The buzzer has its − and + terminals marked. The drawing gives no voltage values.
figures.original: A 1.5 V cell is used with a 3 V buzzer. Will the buzzer work? Explain your answer.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Two drawings of a bean-shaped yellow seed. The left one is the whole seed with a 'food store' label pointing to the yellow body and a 'scar where seed was joined to fruit' label pointing to a small mark on its edge. The right one is a cross-section with a thin brown 'seed coat' around the outside and a small green 'embryo' at the top, next to the yellow interior.
labels: scar where seed was joined to fruit
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: Draw and label the inside parts of the seed.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed 'Name', 'How the plants looked' and 'Growth of plants in cm'. Ashok: green and healthy, 25. Marco: lighter green and quite healthy, 18. Leo: dry and brown, 6. Tariq: thin and weak, 14.
figures.original: Draw a bar chart of the results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Two potted plants are drawn side by side. The left plant has a single bent stem that droops over, with a few yellow, wilted leaves and no flowers. The right plant has several large, bright green rounded leaves and two clusters of red flowers on upright stems.
figures.original: Look at these pictures. Which plant is healthy and growing well?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Two drawings of the same red-flowered geranium plant in a brown pot, labelled Plant A and Plant B. Plant A sits on a windowsill in front of a glass window, with a sun in the upper right pane. Plant B sits inside a dark, closed-in space with a yellow door open beside it, so it is in a dark cupboard-like place.
figures.original: Look at the pictures to see what to do.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Two separate tables side by side. Column A lists five numbered words: 1 seed, 2 embryo, 3 seed coat, 4 germinate, 5 environment. Column B lists five lettered meanings: A the outer cover that protects the seed, B when a seed start to grow, C everything around us, D part of a plant that can grow into a new plant, E part of a seed that grows into a new plant.
labels: the outer cover that protects the seed
when a seed start to grow
part of a plant that can grow into a new plant
part of a seed that grows into a new plant
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: Match the words in column A with their meanings in column B.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of a germinating seed, yellow and rounded like a maize grain, with four parts marked by numbered label lines. Label 1 points to the thin green shoot growing up from the top of the seed. Label 2 points to the large yellow body of the seed. Label 3 points to a small orange-brown part at the bottom of the seed. Label 4 points to a pale root growing downward from the base of the seed.
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: Here is a picture of a germinating seed. Write down the names of parts 1 to 4.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed "Conditions" and "Number of seeds germinated". The rows are: warm, light = 10; warm, dark = 15; cold, light = 5; cold, dark = 7.
figures.original: Dembe's class germinated seeds under different conditions. These are their results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of a branch of a bush willow with green leaves. Several reddish-brown seeds hang from thin stalks along the branch, and each seed has a papery, wing-like outer part surrounding a small green central body. The caption reads 'Bush willow seed.'
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: How do think the bush willow seed is dispersed? Give a reason for your answer.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of two grass-like flower spikes, probably wheat or barley, on a dark background. Each spike has long thin bristles (awns) at the tip. Many small yellow stamens hang down from along the sides of each spike. The photograph is labelled A.
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: Look at the pictures of the two flowers.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of a single carnation flower with many frilly-edged petals. The petals are white with pink-red streaks and stripes. A short green stem is visible at the lower right, and the background is blurred green and yellow. The letter B is printed below the photograph.
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: Look at the pictures of the two flowers.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Two drawings labelled A and B. A shows a winged seed (like a sycamore or maple fruit) with two flat, pale, wing-like parts joined at a green centre with a small stalk on top. B shows an open green pod with round seeds inside and several seeds falling out, with curly tendrils at the bottom.
figures.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
figures.original: How are the seeds shown in the pictures spread? Give a reason for your answers.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A diagram split by a thick orange vertical wall. On the left, a sun with short wavy lines around it sits above a glass of water, and the glass casts a grey shadow on the ground. On the right, a grey shaded area, where the sun does not reach, holds an identical glass of water. Each glass has a line marking the starting water level, and the water in both glasses looks about the same height. There are no printed labels or values.
figures.original: Which glass had the least water and which glass had the most water after two days? Suggest reasons for this.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of a flat wooden rack with a mesh base divided into six sections. Bunches of green grapes lie on the mesh, and a few loose grapes are in one section. A bright yellow sun with rays is drawn above the rack. The caption reads 'grapes drying on a rack in the sun'.
figures.original: Talk about how evaporation happens in each of the pictures and how it is useful.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of a front-loading tumble dryer with its door open. Inside the drum are brightly coloured clothes in pink, green and yellow. The caption underneath reads 'using a tumble dryer'.
figures.original: Talk about how evaporation happens in each of the pictures and how it is useful.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: A diagram of the water cycle. A sun is at top left, and wavy arrows rise from the sea toward a white cloud, with label line A pointing to the arrows. A block arrow points from the white cloud to a grey rain cloud, with label line B pointing to the arrow. Rain falls from the grey cloud onto green mountains with a snow-capped peak, and a small white cloud beside the peak drops snow or hail, with label line C pointing to that cloud. A river runs down the land into the sea, and label line D points to the green land.
figures.original: Label the processes that take place at points A-D on the diagram of the water cycle.

figures.shows: Two upright rectangular mirrors are joined along a vertical edge at a right angle, forming a corner. A yellow coin lies on the surface at the bottom of the corner where the two mirrors meet. No labels or values are printed.
figures.original: Arrange the two mirrors upright and at right angles to each other. Place your small object where the two mirrors meet.

figures.shows: A cartoon-style outdoor scene with a bright yellow sun with rays in the sky at upper right. A red car is parked on grey ground in the middle, a street lamp stands at the left, and a man in a green shirt stands at the right. No shadows are drawn and there are no labels.
figures.original: Identify the source of light in the picture.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 5 Learners Book
figures.shows: Three separate drawings, each on a colored square, with short lines around the top to show that it gives out light. On the left (yellow) is a lit candle with a flame, standing in a candle holder with a curled handle. In the middle (red) is a blue gas canister lamp with a glowing white shade above it. On the right (green) is a table lamp with a lampshade, a glowing bulb inside, a long stand, a round base and an electric cable.
figures.original: Identify the light sources in the pictures.

figures.shows: A tall rectangular periscope tube is drawn with a mirror set at an angle at the top and another at the bottom. A horizontal arrow enters a small window near the top, a vertical arrow labelled 'direction of light' runs down the inside of the tube, and a horizontal arrow leaves a window near the bottom toward an eye on the right. The label 'mirror' has a line pointing to the top mirror.
figures.original: Put these statements A, B, C and D, about how a periscope works, in the correct order.

figures.shows: A horizontal strip divided into five equal rectangles that go from white on the left to very dark grey on the right. Shade 1 is white, shade 2 is light grey, shade 3 is medium grey, shade 4 is dark grey and shade 5 is the darkest, almost black. Each rectangle has its number printed below it.
figures.original: Predict the amount of shadow each material will produce when you shine a light. Use the shade key 1–5.
